title: The Reformed Country-Collector
script: Host: [thoughtful] My guest today has visited over ninety countries, yet argues that most of us are travelling entirely the wrong way. Explain that.
Guest: Gladly, though it'll sound hypocritical coming from someone with a passport this full. I used to collect countries like trophies.
Guest: I realised I could describe fifteen airports in vivid detail, yet barely remember a single conversation I'd had with a local person.
Host: [reflective] So the volume of places was, in some sense, crowding out the depth of the experience?
Guest: Exactly. Ticking off a bucket list rewards speed, whereas actually understanding a place demands the opposite, patience.
Host: [honestly] Isn't that a fairly comfortable philosophy for someone who's already ticked off ninety countries, though?
Guest: That's a fair criticism, and I've heard it before. I'm not saying bucket lists are worthless, only that they were never the whole point.
Host: [gently] What does slow travel actually look like in practice, for someone with limited holiday time?
Guest: Fewer destinations per trip, for a start. I'd rather spend a week in one neighbourhood than a day each in seven cities.
Host: [calmly] Doesn't that risk missing places you might genuinely regret never seeing?
Guest: Possibly, and I've made peace with that trade-off. Missing something is preferable to remembering nothing clearly.
Host: [encouraging] Has slow travel changed how locals respond to you, compared with your earlier trips?
Guest: Enormously. Staying longer means shopkeepers start recognising you, which opens conversations a rushed itinerary never could.
Host: [seriously] What would you tell someone planning their very first big trip?
Guest: Choose fewer places than you think you want, since the version of the trip you imagine rarely matches what actually enriches you.
Host: Practical, if slightly uncomfortable, advice. Thank you for joining us today.
Guest: Thank you for having me, and for indulging a reformed country-collector.

quiz.question: What claim does the guest make despite having visited over ninety countries?
options: Most people are travelling the wrong way
Everyone should visit as many countries as possible
Bucket lists are the best way to travel
Airports are the most interesting part of travel
quiz.explanation: Despite his extensive travel, the guest argues that most people are travelling entirely the wrong way.

quiz.question: What realization made the guest reconsider his approach to travel?
options: He ran out of money
He got lost too often
He could describe airports vividly but barely remembered conversations with local people
He disliked flying
quiz.explanation: He realized he could describe fifteen airports in detail but barely remembered a single conversation with a local person.

quiz.question: How does the host challenge the guest's philosophy?
options: She points out it's a comfortable philosophy for someone who's already visited ninety countries
She says slow travel is too expensive
She says he is lying about his travels
She refuses to discuss the topic further
quiz.explanation: The host challenges him, noting his philosophy is easy to hold once he's already ticked off ninety countries.

quiz.question: What trade-off does the guest accept with slow travel?
options: Spending more money per trip
Never travelling again
Only visiting one country in his life
Possibly missing places he might regret never seeing, in exchange for clearer memories
quiz.explanation: He accepts that he might miss places he'd regret not seeing, but prefers that to remembering nothing clearly.

quiz.question: What advice does the guest give for someone planning their first big trip?
options: Visit as many countries as possible in one trip
Only travel with a tour group
Choose fewer places than you think you want
Avoid talking to locals
quiz.explanation: He advises choosing fewer places than you think you want, since the imagined trip rarely matches what actually enriches you.

quiz.question: What did the traveller realise after visiting more than ninety countries?
options: He waved it off, saying he'd missed enough trains himself to know exactly how that particular panic feels
He remembered airports better than conversations with local people.
Tonight we're discussing awkward cultural misunderstandings abroad
She saw where it would appear and excluded her child.
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: He remembered airports better than conversations with local people.

quiz.question: Why can a bucket list reduce the depth of travel?
options: Hospitals and trains, he said, both strip away pretence
It rewards speed while understanding requires patience.
So, on the last day of a walking tour, I handed our guide a fairly generous tip
Short stays increased water use, rubbish, and unrealistic demands.
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: It rewards speed while understanding requires patience.

quiz.question: What does slower travel look like in his current practice?
options: He texted a month later, simply to say his father had recovered
I'd assumed generosity was generosity, regardless of how it was delivered, which turned out to be naive
The impacts were collective and larger than one visitor's choices.
He spends longer in fewer neighbourhoods instead of racing between cities.
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: He spends longer in fewer neighbourhoods instead of racing between cities.

quiz.question: Which trade-off has he accepted in changing his style?
options: Missing some destinations is preferable to remembering none clearly.
I got the job, as it happens
Thanks so much for sharing it with us
They included signs of the community rather than an empty private stage.
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: Missing some destinations is preferable to remembering none clearly.

quiz.question: How does staying longer improve contact with residents?
options: A stranger wedged his bag into the door gap and held it until she caught up
Repeated encounters allow recognition and more meaningful conversation.
Hopefully it saves someone else an awkward moment on their own trip
Paths, roofs, and cultivated land showed the lived environment.
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: Repeated encounters allow recognition and more meaningful conversation.
